title: Generative Adversarial Networks
authors: Ian J. Goodfellow, Jean Pouget-Abadie, Mehdi Mirza, Bing Xu, David Warde-Farley, Sherjil Ozair, Aaron Courville, Yoshua Bengio

blocks.html: Generative modeling means: given samples from some unknown distribution $p_{\text{data}}$, learn to produce new samples from that distribution. Before GANs, the dominant approaches were either explicit (VAEs, Boltzmann machines, autoregressive models) — they model the density directly — or implicit but limited (RBMs, stochastic Markov chains).
GANs reframe generation as a two-player minimax game:

items: A generator $G(z)$ turns noise $z \sim p_z$ into a synthetic sample.
A discriminator $D(x)$ tries to tell whether $x$ came from $p_{\text{data}}$ or from $G$.

blocks.html: $D$ trains to be good at distinguishing; $G$ trains to fool $D$. At equilibrium, $G$ matches $p_{\text{data}}$ so well that $D$ can do no better than chance: $D(x) = 1/2$ everywhere.
$D$ maximizes the objective: $\log D(x)$ goes up when $D$ correctly labels real samples as real; $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ goes up when $D$ correctly labels fakes as fake.
$G$ minimizes the objective: it can only influence the second term, and pushes $D(G(z))$ toward 1 — making fakes look real.

Theoretical result (paper's Theorem 1): at the global optimum of this minimax game, $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$ exactly, and $D = 1/2$ everywhere. The proof rewrites the value function as a Jensen-Shannon divergence and shows JSD is minimized iff distributions are equal.

items: Sample a mini-batch of real $x$ and noise $z$. Take $k$ gradient ascent steps on $D$ (paper uses $k=1$ in practice).
Sample fresh noise $z$. Take one gradient descent step on $G$.

blocks.html: Non-saturating trick. The minimax loss for $G$ — $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ — saturates when $D$ is confidently rejecting fakes (the gradient is very small exactly when $G$ needs the most help). The paper recommends the practical alternative: train $G$ to maximize $\log D(G(z))$ instead. Same fixed point, much better gradients.

The original paper benchmarks on MNIST, Toronto Face Database, and CIFAR-10. The networks are MLPs (no convolutions — that's DCGAN, two years later). Samples are clearly recognizable as their respective categories, though far from photorealistic.
Quantitatively, log-likelihood is estimated with a Parzen window method (which the authors caveat as imperfect). The samples are most convincing on MNIST.
Pros: no explicit likelihood needed; sharp samples (unlike VAE's blurry ones, because there's no per-pixel mean-squared reconstruction loss); samples are obtained by a single forward pass.

Cons: training is fundamentally a saddle-point problem and is notoriously unstable. Mode collapse — $G$ producing very few distinct samples — was the central failure mode that motivated years of follow-up work (Wasserstein GAN, spectral normalization, gradient penalty, two-time-scale updates, progressive growing, StyleGAN).

GANs dominated image generation from 2015 (DCGAN) through 2021 (StyleGAN3) until diffusion models took over. They remain important for face synthesis, style transfer, and any setting where you need sharp, single-shot samples.
